Name: robust_multigene_qpcr_panels
Title: Robust Multi-Gene qPCR Marker Panels for Cell-Fraction Quantification
Experiment: Improve the current marker-panel selection strategy so that multi-gene qPCR panels provide more reliable quantitative cell-fraction estimation than the best single-marker baseline. Focus on robustness rather than only maximizing ROC AUC. Investigate marker combinations that reduce prediction error across low, medium, and high target-cell fractions while keeping the number of selected marker genes small. The method should continue to use discovery cells for marker selection and held-out cells for final evaluation. Reference genes should be used for normalization rather than as a competing classifier. Evaluate the proposed method using held-out ROC AUC, Spearman correlation between true and predicted cell fraction, MAE, RMSE, low-fraction MAE, high-fraction MAE, and marker-panel size. Compare directly against the current best-single-marker baseline and the existing greedy multi-gene baseline. Do not introduce data leakage between discovery and held-out cells.

Name: confounder_invariant_qpcr_panels
Title: Confounder-Invariant qPCR Marker Panels for Cell-Fraction Quantification
Experiment: Add a nuisance-augmented panel-selection and stress-testing framework using only the provided H5AD dataset. First retain the existing discovery/holdout cell split and discovery-only marker ranking. Extend pseudobulk simulation so that each mixture can optionally undergo fixed, reproducible perturbations: global RNA scaling, gene-wise multiplicative assay efficiency variation, zero inflation or dropout, ambient-RNA contamination from randomly sampled background cells, and alternative background-cluster compositions. Define several nuisance regimes and sample nuisance parameters independently for training and testing. Generate augmented training pseudobulks from discovery cells and independently generated nominal and perturbed test pseudobulks from holdout cells. Implement a new robust panel objective that combines cross-validated quantitative error across fraction bins with a worst-case penalty across nuisance regimes, for example mean MAE plus lambda times the maximum regime-specific MAE. Select panels greedily or by forward selection from the discovery-ranked candidates, with a small panel-size penalty and a fixed maximum of five markers. Optionally filter or rank reference genes by stability not only across clusters but also under simulated global scaling, dropout, and ambient contamination; references must remain normalization-only and must not be selected as markers. Add evaluation for the best single marker, the current nominal greedy panel, and the new confounder-robust panel. Report overall and regime-specific ROC AUC, sensitivity at fixed specificity, specificity at the detection threshold, MAE, RMSE, Spearman correlation, Pearson correlation, R2, calibration slope/intercept, low- and high-fraction MAE, and worst-case MAE. Use independently seeded simulations and do not tune perturbation parameters on the held-out results. Generate ROC plots by nuisance regime, predicted-versus-true fraction plots colored by fraction bin, error-versus-fraction curves, a heatmap of MAE across panel methods and perturbations, and a panel-size versus worst-case-error Pareto plot. Include ablations showing the contribution of each nuisance type and compare nominal-only selection with robust selection. The key hypothesis is that nuisance-robust multi-gene panels will retain competitive nominal performance while reducing error inflation, false positives, and loss of sensitivity under technical and background-composition shifts.

Name: compositional_identifiability_qpcr
Title: Identifiability-Aware Joint qPCR Panels for Compositional Cell-Fraction Deconvolution
Experiment: Extend the existing discovery/holdout framework from one-target-versus-rest prediction to simultaneous estimation of all cluster proportions. Using discovery cells only, compute cluster-specific mean expression signatures for candidate genes after reference-gene normalization. Construct a joint signature matrix and select a small set of genes per cluster using a forward-selection objective that combines target discrimination, low within-panel redundancy, and signature identifiability, measured by condition number, pairwise cosine similarity, or the smallest singular value of the normalized signature matrix. Exclude reference genes from marker selection. For each held-out pseudobulk mixture, estimate all cluster fractions jointly using non-negative least squares or constrained linear regression with fractions constrained to be non-negative and sum to one. Fit the model only on discovery-derived signatures and evaluate on independently generated holdout pseudobulks. Retain the existing best-single-marker and one-vs-rest greedy panels as baselines, evaluated on the same mixtures. Add simulations that vary target abundance, background-cluster composition, and the similarity of related clusters by sampling mixtures from Dirichlet distributions with different concentration parameters. Include rare-target regimes below 1%, 5%, and 10%, and high-abundance regimes above 50%. Report per-cluster and aggregate ROC AUC, sensitivity at fixed specificity, MAE, RMSE, Spearman correlation, Pearson correlation, R2, calibration slope/intercept, fraction bias, compositional closure error, and the rate at which estimated fractions are exactly or approximately non-negative and sum to one. Quantify cross-cell-type confusion with a true-versus-predicted fraction heatmap and evaluate whether errors are concentrated among biologically similar clusters. Use bootstrap resampling of held-out pseudobulks to generate confidence intervals for metrics. Generate plots including signature-matrix heatmaps, marker-panel similarity and condition-number comparisons, predicted-versus-true fraction plots, simplex/closure-error plots, cluster confusion heatmaps, error versus true abundance curves, and Pareto plots of panel size versus aggregate error and identifiability. Add an ablation comparing discrimination-only selection, redundancy-aware selection, and full identifiability-aware selection. The principal hypothesis is that jointly designed panels will produce more coherent and interpretable fraction estimates, reduce cross-cluster misattribution, and reveal an empirical limit of quantification for closely related or poorly identifiable cell types.

Name: uncertainty_calibrated_qpcr_panels
Title: Uncertainty-Calibrated qPCR Marker Panels with Empirical Limits of Detection and Quantification
Experiment: Extend the existing discovery/holdout pipeline so that marker selection and uncertainty calibration are separated. Retain the cluster-stratified cell split and discovery-only Wilcoxon marker ranking. Divide independently generated discovery pseudobulks into a panel-selection set and a calibration set. Select the best single marker and the current greedy multi-gene panel as baselines. Add an uncertainty-aware forward-selection method that evaluates a candidate panel using both cross-validated fraction MAE and uncertainty criteria, such as calibration-set residual scale, rare-fraction error, and prediction-interval width, with a small panel-size penalty. Fit the fraction model on the panel-selection data and use the calibration pseudobulks to construct split-conformal prediction intervals: compute absolute residuals, estimate a finite-sample quantile, and generate clipped intervals for held-out predictions. Optionally implement a residual bootstrap alternative to quantify uncertainty arising from cell resampling and model fitting. Add a simulation layer for finite-cell sampling, global RNA scaling, gene-wise assay noise, dropout, ambient RNA contamination, and altered background-cluster composition, with perturbation parameters fixed before evaluating the held-out data. Generate test pseudobulks across explicit abundance regimes, including 0 to 1 percent, 1 to 5 percent, 5 to 10 percent, 10 to 50 percent, and above 50 percent target cells, while varying cells per pseudobulk. Evaluate point metrics already present in the code, together with empirical prediction-interval coverage at 80 percent and 95 percent nominal levels, mean interval width, coverage by abundance bin, calibration slope and intercept, bias, false-positive rate for nominally absent or very-low target cells, false-negative rate at the detection threshold, and the lowest abundance satisfying predefined coverage and MAE criteria. Define an operational assay decision rule with three outcomes: below detection, detected but not reliably quantifiable, and quantifiable. Estimate the limit of detection as the smallest target fraction achieving a specified sensitivity at fixed specificity, and the limit of quantification as the smallest fraction achieving nominal interval coverage plus an MAE or relative-error threshold. Use bootstrap resampling of held-out pseudobulks to obtain confidence intervals for coverage, detection limits, and panel comparisons. Generate ROC and precision-recall curves for rare-target detection, predicted-versus-true plots with prediction intervals, interval-width-versus-abundance curves, coverage-versus-abundance plots, calibration diagrams, error distributions by nuisance regime, and Pareto plots of panel size versus MAE, interval width, and detection/quantification limit. Include ablations comparing uncalibrated point estimates, bootstrap intervals, conformal intervals, nominal greedy selection, and uncertainty-aware selection. Do not tune the conformal quantile, detection thresholds, or limit criteria on the held-out results. The main hypothesis is that uncertainty-calibrated panels will provide more trustworthy rare-cell measurements by identifying an empirical quantification limit and reducing overconfident calls, even when their average point-estimation error is similar to nominally optimized panels.

Name: biological_state_invariant_panels
Title: Biological-State-Invariant qPCR Marker Panels for Robust Cell-Type Quantification
Experiment: Extend the discovery/holdout workflow to model biological heterogeneity within each Leiden cluster. First, retain the existing cluster-stratified cell split and discovery-only marker ranking. Within each discovery cluster, construct a state representation using normalized expression or log-transformed expression after excluding all ranked marker candidates, reference genes, mitochondrial genes, ribosomal genes, and other globally ubiquitous genes. Compute PCA and define two to four reproducible latent state strata per sufficiently large cluster using k-means or hierarchical clustering, with a minimum number of cells per stratum. State definitions must be learned only from discovery cells. Quantify within-cluster state heterogeneity for every candidate gene using between-state variance, state effect size, and expression detection-rate differences. Add a state-aware pseudobulk simulator that samples target cells either from the overall cluster distribution, from individual latent states, or from deliberately shifted state mixtures such as state-enriched target populations. Generate training pseudobulks from discovery cells using leave-one-state-out or state-balanced designs, and generate independent nominal and state-shifted test pseudobulks from held-out cells. Implement a new panel-selection objective that combines cross-validated quantitative MAE, worst-state MAE, low-fraction MAE, and a marker-state-instability penalty. For example, select panels using mean_state_MAE plus lambda times the maximum state-specific MAE plus gamma times the average normalized state variance, with a small panel-size penalty and a maximum of five markers. Reference genes remain normalization-only; they should be filtered or ranked for stability across both clusters and latent biological states. Compare the proposed state-invariant panel against the existing nominal greedy multi-gene panel and the best single-marker baseline, all evaluated on identical held-out mixtures. Report overall and state-specific ROC AUC, precision-recall AUC for rare targets, sensitivity at fixed specificity, specificity at the detection threshold, MAE, RMSE, Spearman and Pearson correlation, R2, calibration slope/intercept, bias, low- and high-fraction MAE, worst-state MAE, and performance degradation between nominal and state-shifted mixtures. Quantify marker robustness using state-effect sizes, coefficient of variation, detection-rate variability, panel overlap across state splits, and the fraction of selected genes that are state-associated. Generate plots including within-cluster state embeddings, state-specific marker-expression heatmaps, candidate state-variance versus discrimination scatterplots, ROC and precision-recall curves by state-shift regime, predicted-versus-true fraction plots colored by target state, absolute error versus target fraction, heatmaps of state-specific MAE, and Pareto plots of panel size versus nominal error and worst-state error. Include ablations comparing discrimination-only selection, state-penalized selection, state-balanced training, and state-balanced plus state-penalized selection. Perform sensitivity analyses over the number of latent states, PCA dimensions, state-shift severity, cells per pseudobulk, dropout, and ambient RNA contamination. Use fixed random seeds and independent discovery/test simulations, and do not tune state definitions or robustness penalties using held-out outcomes. The key hypothesis is that selecting markers that are quantitatively informative across latent biological states will reduce failure under activation or maturation shifts, especially at low target abundance, while preserving competitive nominal performance and requiring only a small qPCR panel.

Name: hierarchical_qpcr_assays
Title: Hierarchical qPCR Marker Panels for Coarse-to-Fine Cell-Type Fraction Quantification
Experiment: Develop a hierarchical assay-design framework using only the provided H5AD dataset. Preserve the existing cluster-stratified discovery/holdout split and perform all hierarchy construction, marker ranking, reference-gene selection, and model fitting using discovery cells only. Compute discovery-derived cluster-level expression signatures after normalization and construct a cluster similarity matrix using correlation or cosine similarity. Build a reproducible hierarchical tree by agglomerative clustering, with sensitivity analyses over the number of top-level lineages and tree-cut thresholds. For every internal node, define a parent-lineage discrimination problem that separates all descendant clusters from non-descendant clusters. For every child split, define a conditional discrimination problem among sibling groups. Rank candidate genes with discovery-only differential expression and select small parent and child marker panels using forward selection optimized for quantitative fraction MAE, redundancy penalties, and specificity against the relevant non-target groups. Reference genes remain normalization-only and are excluded from all marker candidates. Add hierarchical pseudobulk simulation in which target fractions, parent-lineage fractions, and sibling composition are independently varied, including near-zero target abundance, rare target within a common lineage, dominant target abundance, and background mixtures enriched for biologically similar clusters. Generate training mixtures from discovery cells and independent nominal and shifted-composition test mixtures from holdout cells. Fit parent fraction models and conditional child fraction models separately, then estimate the target fraction as the clipped product of the parent estimate and conditional child estimate. Compare hierarchical assays against the existing flat best-single-marker panel, flat greedy panel, and optionally a joint non-negative deconvolution baseline on identical held-out mixtures. Report overall and per-cluster ROC AUC, rare-target precision-recall AUC, sensitivity at fixed specificity, MAE, RMSE, Spearman correlation, Pearson correlation, R2, bias, low- and high-fraction MAE, parent-fraction error, conditional-fraction error, product-propagation error, false-positive rates against non-lineage backgrounds, and panel size. Quantify error amplification through the hierarchy and identify clusters for which hierarchical estimation improves or worsens performance. Perform bootstrap confidence intervals over held-out pseudobulks and sensitivity analyses over tree depth, cells per pseudobulk, target abundance, and sibling similarity. Generate plots including the discovery-derived cluster dendrogram, lineage marker heatmaps, hierarchy diagrams annotated with selected genes, ROC and precision-recall curves for flat versus hierarchical panels, predicted-versus-true fraction plots, parent-versus-child error decomposition plots, error-versus-abundance curves, related-cluster false-positive heatmaps, and panel-size versus quantitative-error Pareto plots. The main hypothesis is that coarse-to-fine marker panels will reduce confusion among related cell types and provide a scalable assay architecture, while revealing conditions under which hierarchical error propagation makes flat panels preferable.

Name: self_validating_qpcr_panels
Title: Self-Validating qPCR Marker Panels with Orthogonal Sentinel Genes and Selective Quantification
Experiment: Extend the discovery/holdout workflow to design assays that can either quantify a target cell fraction or explicitly abstain when the estimate is unsupported. Preserve the cluster-stratified discovery/holdout split and ensure that marker, reference, sentinel, and model parameters are learned only from discovery cells. First rank target marker candidates using discovery-only differential expression as in the current code. Select stable reference genes using the existing normalization procedure, excluding all marker and sentinel genes. Add a separate sentinel-gene selection stage from genes that are not references or target markers. Sentinel candidates should be chosen to provide orthogonal information about background composition, marker disagreement, or model misspecification rather than direct target discrimination. Candidate criteria can include low correlation with the target score, high variation across background clusters, and strong association with residuals from discovery pseudobulk models. Generate discovery pseudobulks with known target fractions and fit the ordinary normalized marker-score fraction model. For every discovery pseudobulk, calculate: the disagreement among single-marker fraction predictions; residuals between observed sentinel expression and discovery-derived background/mixture signatures; distance to the convex hull or robust covariance distribution of supported pseudobulk expression profiles; and a sentinel consistency score. Combine these features into a QC score using a simple discovery-only logistic model for unreliable samples, where unreliable training examples are created by simulated perturbations such as target-free mixtures, ambient RNA contamination, dropout, gene-wise efficiency variation, global scaling, altered background-cluster composition, and marker-specific corruption. Alternatively, use an unsupervised quantile-based acceptance rule to avoid dependence on arbitrary simulated labels. Optimize marker-plus-sentinel panels using a selective-risk objective: minimize MAE among accepted samples, penalize false acceptance of high-error samples, and impose a minimum coverage or retention constraint. Keep the maximum number of quantitative markers small, for example five, and allow one to three sentinel genes. Compare four methods on identical held-out pseudobulks: the existing best single marker, the existing nominal greedy panel, a robust multi-gene panel without abstention, and the proposed self-validating panel with QC rejection. Evaluate nominal and perturbed holdout regimes separately, including explicit target fractions below 1%, 1%-5%, 5%-10%, 10%-50%, and above 50%. Report ordinary held-out ROC AUC, MAE, RMSE, Spearman correlation, Pearson correlation, R2, low- and high-fraction MAE, and calibration slope/intercept. Add selective metrics including risk-coverage curves, conditional MAE and RMSE at each retained-sample fraction, rejection rate, false-acceptance rate for samples exceeding a predefined error threshold, rejection AUC for unreliable versus reliable samples, target-free false-positive rate, detection sensitivity at fixed specificity, and the fraction of samples classified as quantifiable, detected-but-unreliable, or below detection. Define QC thresholds using only a discovery calibration subset and do not tune them on held-out results. Use bootstrap resampling of held-out pseudobulks to obtain confidence intervals for conditional error, coverage, rejection AUC, and false-acceptance rates. Generate plots including marker-versus-sentinel disagreement scatterplots, sentinel and residual heatmaps, ROC curves for target detection and reliability detection, risk-coverage curves, conditional MAE-versus-coverage plots, predicted-versus-true fractions colored by QC status, error-versus-fraction curves, reliability calibration diagrams, and a heatmap of acceptance rates across nuisance regimes. Perform ablations removing marker disagreement, removing sentinel residuals, removing expression-distance features, and replacing the learned QC rule with a simple fixed threshold. Also assess sensitivity to the number of sentinels, cells per pseudobulk, perturbation severity, and the threshold defining an unacceptable quantitative error. The principal hypothesis is that orthogonal sentinel genes and selective abstention will reduce harmful overconfident estimates under rare-cell, composition-shift, and technical perturbation regimes, while preserving competitive nominal performance and requiring only a modest increase in assay size.

Name: rna_yield_aware_cell_fraction_assays
Title: RNA-Yield-Aware qPCR Panels for Distinguishing Cell Fraction from Transcript Fraction
Experiment:
Extend the existing discovery/holdout framework with an explicit cell-specific RNA-yield model. Preserve the cluster-stratified discovery/holdout split and ensure that RNA-yield estimation, marker selection, reference-gene selection, and calibration are learned only from discovery cells. First inspect available count-related information in adata.obs, such as n_counts, total_counts, library size, or equivalent fields. If raw counts are available, estimate per-cell RNA yield from total counts; otherwise use a reproducible proxy based on pre-normalization library size or expression total, with sensitivity analyses over proxy definitions. Estimate cluster-specific mean RNA yield, within-cluster coefficient of variation, and robust quantiles of RNA yield. Explicitly report that these are proxies for RNA content rather than direct physical measurements.

Add an RNA-yield-aware pseudobulk simulator. For each simulated sample, draw target and background cells as before to define the true cell fraction, but weight each sampled cell's expression contribution by its simulated RNA yield before aggregating. Normalize mixtures to equal total RNA input, so the observed molecular composition reflects RNA-weighted rather than cell-weighted abundance. Include independent regimes with homogeneous RNA yield, discovery-estimated heterogeneous yield, target-enriched high-yield cells, target-enriched low-yield cells, background-enriched high-yield cells, and shifts in target-to-background RNA-yield ratios at test time. Vary cells per pseudobulk and explicitly include target fractions below 1%, 1%-5%, 5%-10%, 10%-50%, and above 50%.

Implement three assay models evaluated on identical held-out mixtures. The first is the current naive normalized marker-score model, interpreted as an RNA-fraction estimator. The second is a yield-calibrated model that maps marker score or estimated RNA fraction to cell fraction using discovery-derived cluster RNA-yield calibration. A simple version can divide the target RNA contribution by the estimated target RNA yield relative to the background yield; a more stable version can fit a discovery-only regression using both marker score and estimated sample-level RNA-yield features, with non-negative and clipped predictions. The third is a robust yield-aware model selected using augmented discovery pseudobulks spanning plausible RNA-yield ratios and within-cluster variability. Keep reference genes normalization-only and exclude them from marker selection.

Modify panel selection to compare the existing single-marker and greedy multi-gene objectives against a yield-aware objective combining cross-validated cell-fraction MAE, absolute bias, low-fraction MAE, and sensitivity to RNA-yield ratio. Penalize panels whose estimates change strongly under simulated RNA-yield perturbations while preserving a small maximum panel size. Do not select markers solely because they correlate with library size; assess and report marker-library-size correlation and exclude genes with strong generic RNA-content dependence when appropriate. Include an ablation comparing equal-cell pseudobulks, RNA-weighted pseudobulks without calibration, yield calibration without robust selection, and full RNA-yield-aware selection.

Evaluate held-out ROC AUC and precision-recall AUC for rare-target detection, sensitivity at fixed specificity, specificity at the operational detection threshold, MAE, RMSE, Spearman and Pearson correlation, R2, calibration slope/intercept, bias, relative error, low- and high-fraction MAE, and error as a function of the target-to-background RNA-yield ratio. Report both cell-fraction error and RNA-fraction error to reveal whether a method is estimating the wrong biological quantity. Define an RNA-yield mismatch stress test in which the test-time target RNA-yield distribution differs from discovery by prespecified multiplicative factors, for example 0.5x, 1x, 2x, and 4x, without tuning these factors on held-out outcomes. Use bootstrap confidence intervals over held-out pseudobulks and paired comparisons between methods.

Generate plots including distributions of RNA-yield proxies by cluster, cluster RNA-yield versus marker expression, true cell fraction versus observed RNA fraction, predicted-versus-true cell fraction plots, prediction bias versus RNA-yield ratio, ROC and precision-recall curves for nominal and RNA-yield-shifted regimes, error-versus-abundance curves, heatmaps of MAE and bias across target abundance and yield mismatch, calibration plots for cell fraction versus RNA fraction, and Pareto plots of panel size versus quantitative error and yield-shift robustness. Include a theoretical or empirical identifiability analysis showing the expected cell-fraction bias of an RNA-fraction estimator as a function of the target/background RNA-yield ratio. The main hypothesis is that strong nominal detection performance can coexist with substantial cell-fraction bias under RNA-content heterogeneity, and that explicit RNA-yield calibration will improve quantitative cell-abundance estimation while identifying regimes in which cell fraction cannot be reliably recovered from equal-RNA qPCR measurements alone.

Name: globally_budgeted_qpcr_panels
Title: Globally Budgeted Multi-Target qPCR Panels for Scalable Cell-Fraction Quantification
Experiment: Develop a shared-assay design framework that selects one globally budgeted set of qPCR genes for quantifying multiple Leiden clusters. Preserve the existing cluster-stratified discovery/holdout split and ensure that all candidate ranking, reference-gene selection, panel optimization, and model fitting use discovery cells or discovery pseudobulks only. First generate independently simulated discovery pseudobulks for every target cluster using the existing simulator, retaining explicit low, medium, and high target-fraction regimes. Build a union of discovery-ranked marker candidates while excluding reference genes from marker selection. Implement several panel-design strategies: (1) independently optimized cluster-specific panels, (2) a shared global gene panel with one regression model per target, (3) a shared panel with target-specific gene subsets, and (4) a fairness-constrained global panel that limits dominance by common or abundant clusters. Use forward selection under total assay budgets such as 5, 10, 15, 20, and 30 genes. At each step, evaluate candidate genes using discovery-only cross-validation across all target clusters. The objective should combine macro quantitative MAE, worst-cluster MAE, low-fraction MAE, macro ROC AUC, rare-target performance, and a redundancy penalty based on feature correlation or similarity of discovery-derived cluster signatures. A weighted or minimax objective should be used so that globally selected genes are not chosen solely for the easiest or most abundant clusters. For the shared panel, fit target-specific linear regression models using normalized marker expression scores or all selected genes, with clipping or non-negative constraints where appropriate. For target-specific subsets, assign each selected gene to the clusters for which it provides the largest validated improvement, while enforcing a maximum subset size per cluster. Keep reference genes shared and normalization-only. Generate one fixed held-out pseudobulk evaluation set per target and compare all methods on identical samples. Include nominal testing and stress tests involving altered background-cluster composition, finite-cell sampling, dropout, ambient RNA contamination, global RNA scaling, and gene-wise assay efficiency perturbations. Report per-cluster and aggregate ROC AUC, precision-recall AUC for rare targets, sensitivity at fixed specificity, specificity at the operational detection threshold, MAE, RMSE, Spearman correlation, Pearson correlation, R2, calibration slope/intercept, bias, low- and high-fraction MAE, worst-cluster error, and the number of clusters meeting predefined assay-quality criteria. Quantify assay efficiency using total number of genes, mean genes per target, fraction of genes shared across targets, and the number of unique primers required. Add a budget-coverage metric defined as the proportion of clusters achieving, for example, AUC >= 0.90 and MAE <= 0.05 at each total gene budget. Use bootstrap resampling of held-out pseudobulks to estimate confidence intervals and paired differences between global and independent designs. Generate plots including performance-versus-total-gene-budget curves, macro-error and worst-cluster-error Pareto fronts, per-cluster MAE heatmaps across budgets and methods, ROC curves for selected representative clusters, gene-sharing networks, cluster-by-gene utility heatmaps, panel overlap diagrams, and assay-budget coverage curves. Include ablations comparing discrimination-only selection, quantitative-error selection, redundancy-aware selection, and fairness-constrained selection. The principal hypothesis is that a compact globally optimized panel can achieve substantially better assay scalability than independently designed panels, while revealing an interpretable trade-off between total primer budget, rare-cell performance, and equitable quantification across biologically distinct cell types.

Name: mixture_law_calibrated_qpcr
Title: Mixture-Law-Aware Calibration of qPCR Marker Panels for Quantitative Cell-Fraction Estimation
Experiment: Develop a calibration-aware extension of the existing discovery/holdout pipeline. Preserve the cluster-stratified cell split, discovery-only Wilcoxon marker ranking, discovery-only reference-gene selection, and independent holdout pseudobulk generation. Replace the assumption that normalized marker expression is linearly related to cell fraction with several explicitly compared calibration models. Implement: (1) the current linear delta-expression baseline; (2) a log-ratio model using log1p marker expression minus the geometric or arithmetic mean of log1p reference expression, mimicking a delta-Ct scale; (3) isotonic regression constrained to produce a monotonic mapping from panel score to fraction; and (4) a low-complexity nonlinear calibration model such as a quadratic or restricted spline regression with clipping and monotonicity checks. Fit all calibration parameters using discovery pseudobulks only, using nested cross-validation for model and panel selection. Select marker panels by forward selection from discovery-ranked candidates with an objective combining cross-validated inverse-prediction MAE, calibration bias, low-fraction MAE, high-fraction MAE, and a small panel-size penalty. Penalize panels whose fitted response curves are non-monotonic, excessively steep, or extrapolate beyond the observed discovery range. Compare mean aggregation of marker scores with robust aggregation such as the median or trimmed mean to assess sensitivity to one poorly behaving marker. Extend pseudobulk simulation with controlled analytical and mixture-law effects: total-RNA dilution or global scaling, finite-cell sampling, target/background transcript-abundance ratios, marker-expression saturation, gene-specific multiplicative assay efficiency, and optional Ct-like transformation using a fixed amplification-efficiency parameter. Sample these nuisance parameters independently in discovery and holdout regimes, with nominal settings defined before evaluation. Evaluate the best single-marker panel, the existing greedy linear panel, and the proposed calibration-aware panels on identical held-out mixtures. Report ROC AUC and precision-recall AUC for rare-target detection, sensitivity at fixed specificity, specificity at the detection threshold, MAE, RMSE, Spearman correlation, Pearson correlation, R2, mean signed bias, relative error, calibration slope and intercept, monotonicity violations, error by abundance bin, and error under total-RNA dilution. Quantify calibration transfer by measuring the change in MAE and bias between nominal and shifted transcript-abundance or assay-efficiency regimes. Add an empirical dynamic-range analysis that identifies the smallest and largest fractions for which the calibrated panel satisfies predefined MAE, relative-error, and bias criteria. Use bootstrap resampling of held-out pseudobulks for confidence intervals and paired comparisons between calibration methods. Generate plots including panel-score-versus-true-fraction calibration curves with confidence bands, predicted-versus-true fraction plots, residual-versus-fraction plots, bias-versus-abundance curves, ROC and precision-recall curves, Bland-Altman-style agreement plots, heatmaps of MAE and bias across abundance and assay-efficiency regimes, response-curve comparisons between linear and nonlinear models, and panel-size-versus-calibration-error Pareto plots. Include ablations removing log-ratio normalization, nonlinear calibration, robust marker aggregation, and mixture-law stress testing. The main hypothesis is that calibration-aware panels will preserve detection performance while substantially reducing systematic quantitative bias at very low and very high target fractions, and that nonlinear or log-ratio mappings will define a more realistic assay dynamic range than a globally linear expression-to-cell-fraction model.

Name: adversarial_background_specificity
Title: Adversarial Background-Aware qPCR Panels for Reliable Cell-Type Quantification
Experiment:
Extend the discovery/holdout framework with explicit adversarial background-composition analysis. Preserve the stratified cell split and ensure that all cluster similarity calculations, candidate ranking, reference-gene selection, panel optimization, and adversarial-mixture construction use discovery cells only. First compute discovery-derived cluster expression signatures using the candidate genes after reference-gene normalization. For each target cluster, quantify similarity between the target and every non-target cluster using cosine similarity, correlation, or standardized signature distance. Define difficult background sets consisting of the most similar non-target clusters, while retaining all other clusters as ordinary backgrounds.

Add a target-free simulator in which the target fraction can be exactly zero, together with rare-target regimes such as 0%, 0.1%-1%, 1%-5%, 5%-10%, 10%-50%, and above 50%. Generate several discovery and held-out background regimes: ordinary Dirichlet mixtures, single-cluster-enriched backgrounds, nearest-neighbor backgrounds, mixtures concentrated on the top two or three similar clusters, and adversarial mixtures selected by searching over a simplex of background proportions. The adversarial search must be performed separately for discovery and holdout simulations. It can maximize the target panel score or false-positive probability subject to a fixed minimum and maximum background contribution, using a reproducible grid, random Dirichlet proposals, or constrained optimization. Holdout adversarial mixtures must use only held-out cells for expression sampling and must not be used to tune the panel.

Implement three panel-selection methods: (1) the current best single marker, (2) the current nominal greedy multi-gene panel optimized by cross-validated MAE under random backgrounds, and (3) an adversarial-specificity panel selected by forward selection. The new objective should combine discovery cross-validated quantitative MAE, low-fraction MAE, target-free false-positive rate, rare-target precision-recall loss, and a worst-background penalty. For example, use mean MAE plus lambda times the maximum MAE across background regimes plus gamma times the maximum target-free score or false-positive rate. Include a small panel-size penalty and a maximum size of five markers. Reference genes remain normalization-only and are excluded from every marker candidate set.

Evaluate all methods on identical nominal and adversarial held-out mixtures. Report per-cluster and macro ROC AUC, precision-recall AUC, sensitivity at fixed specificity, specificity at the operational detection threshold, target-free false-positive rate, false-positive rate by background cluster, false-negative rate near the detection threshold, MAE, RMSE, bias, Spearman correlation, Pearson correlation, R2, low- and high-fraction MAE, worst-background MAE, worst-background false-positive rate, and panel size. Quantify the specificity-quantification trade-off by comparing nominal performance with worst-case performance and by measuring the degradation caused by replacing random backgrounds with nearest-neighbor backgrounds.

Generate plots including ROC and precision-recall curves for nominal versus adversarial backgrounds, background-cluster-by-panel false-positive heatmaps, target-free panel-score distributions, predicted-versus-true fraction plots colored by background regime, MAE and bias versus target fraction, worst-case error versus average error scatterplots, panel-size versus worst-case specificity Pareto plots, and cluster-signature similarity maps annotated with selected markers. Add ablations comparing random-background selection, similarity-aware selection, target-free-aware selection, and the full adversarial objective. Perform sensitivity analyses over the number of adversarial proposals, similarity metric, maximum background concentration, cells per pseudobulk, and the detection threshold. Use bootstrap resampling of held-out pseudobulks to estimate confidence intervals for paired differences in worst-case false-positive rate and quantitative error. The main hypothesis is that panels selected against biologically plausible adversarial backgrounds will sacrifice little nominal performance while substantially reducing false positives and quantitative bias caused by closely related non-target cell types.
